fatal_flaws: Hidden structural twin of the crowded 'policy simulator / AI impact dashboard' archetype: natural-language rule in, before/after charts out, plain-English brief. Without a uniquely constrained domain or proprietary workflow integration, judges may read it as a polished civic-tech dashboard rather than a new mechanism.

The core depends on fragile live LLM parsing. If the parser turns a parliamentarian's rule into the wrong predicates, the demo either silently misleads or exposes that the product cannot safely handle the very ambiguity it claims to solve.

ChatGPT-replaceable surface is high. A generic chatbot plus a spreadsheet can already summarize a proposed rule, list assumptions, and produce caveats. The proposed hard-to-fake advantage only survives if the executable predicates and attribution are visibly rigorous, not just JSON-shaped LLM output.

The data claims are inherently unverifiable because the baseline dataset is synthetic. The demo can show internal consistency, but it cannot prove real-world policy consequence validity, constituency relevance, distributional fairness, or administrative feasibility.

Demo theatre risk is severe: changing one sentence and watching charts move is visually convincing even if the predicates, uncertainty bands, and segment deltas are hand-tuned around a small fixture. Judges may discount it as an impressive toy model.

Sponsor and event fit are weak. EasyA/Web3 context is mostly audience decoration; there is no sponsor SDK, blockchain primitive, or venue-specific capability materially improving the system. The technology role text even treats the in-person venue as if it were part of the core mechanism, which is a credibility smell.

Uncertainty ranges may look scientific without a defensible statistical model. On a generated fixture, uncertainty is likely arbitrary sensitivity analysis rather than calibrated uncertainty, which creates overclaim risk in exactly the institutional setting the concept targets.
survive_if: Narrow the demo to one concrete fictional policy domain with a published schema, deterministic rule DSL, and 3-5 rule types the system can parse reliably.
Make the LLM produce a constrained intermediate representation that users can edit before simulation, with validation failures shown clearly instead of forcing every natural-language input through.
Replace broad 'policy consequence' claims with 'scenario consistency check on a declared synthetic baseline' and label uncertainty as sensitivity bounds, not prediction.
Add adversarial demo cases where unsupported or ambiguous rule text is rejected, so the product proves restraint rather than only producing attractive output.
Show an audit trail from source fields to predicates to affected records to aggregate deltas, with at least one judge-edited rule that was not pre-scripted.
Tie the pitch to a real last-mile parliamentary workflow, such as scrutiny questions or committee brief preparation, rather than a generic impact dashboard.
backup_reason: The backup has a stronger hard-to-fake action: it verifies a correction, writes workflow state, and produces a tamper-evident receipt. Its crypto/provenance role is materially connected to the outcome, while the primary risks being a synthetic policy dashboard with LLM-generated explanations.
